words.meaning_en: A strong exclamation, like 'damn!' — from 'tabernacle'. Very Quebecois, very vulgar in polite company.
A softened, polite version of a swear word — like 'darn' or 'shoot'. Safe to use anywhere.
A strong swear word, from 'calice' (chalice). Common, but vulgar.
A strong swear word, from 'hostie' (the communion host). Vulgar.
A strong swear word, from 'Christ'. Vulgar, but extremely common in informal speech.

words.example_qc: Ça va te coûter dix piasses.
words.meaning_en: A dollar. 'Piasse' is the familiar Quebec word for a dollar, from the old Spanish piastre.

words.example_qc: Prends mon char, c'est plus vite.
words.meaning_en: A car. In Quebec, 'char' means car, not a chariot — don't be confused.
To go shopping. A Quebec verb made from English 'magazine' (to shop) — perfectly normal here.
Here. 'Icitte' is the familiar Quebec pronunciation/spelling of 'ici'.
Now, right now. From 'à cette heure' (at this hour).
Well. 'Ben' is 'bien' said fast, used constantly as a filler word.
Cold. 'Frette' is the Quebec familiar word for cold weather.

words.example_en: I'll stop at the corner store for milk.
words.example_qc: Je vais arrêter au dépanneur pour du lait.
words.meaning_en: A corner convenience store. The most Quebecois shop there is — open late, sells almost everything.

words.example_en: Put on your winter hat, it's -20.
words.meaning_en: A knitted winter hat. 'Tuque' is Canadian, and essential in Quebec winter.

words.example_en: My girlfriend is from Quebec City.
words.meaning_en: Girlfriend (familiar). 'Blonde' literally means blonde, but here it means your girlfriend, whatever her hair colour.
Boyfriend, or a male buddy. Context tells you which — 'mon chum' is usually your boyfriend.
Silly, dumb, goofy. A mild, familiar insult — not very mean.
To cry, or to whine/complain. 'Brailler' is stronger than 'pleurer' in tone.

words.example_qc: On a jasé pendant une heure.
words.meaning_en: To chat, to talk. 'Jaser' is the Quebec verb for a good chat.

words.example_qc: On va prendre un cinq à sept?
words.meaning_en: After-work drinks, literally 5 to 7 p.m. A Quebec social institution.
It's all good, perfect, sorted. A cheerful, old-fashioned Quebec expression.

words.example_en: We had so much fun at the cabin.
words.example_qc: On a eu du fun au chalet.
words.meaning_en: To have fun. 'Avoir du fun' is an anglicism that is completely normal in Quebec French.

words.example_en: Grab a coffee on your way.
words.meaning_en: To grab, catch, or get. 'Pogner' is very versatile — and very Quebecois.

words.example_en: He's just slacking off all day.
words.example_qc: Il se pogne le beigne toute la journée.
words.meaning_en: To do nothing, to slack off. Literally 'to grab yourself the donut'. Familiar, funny, not polite at work.
Not at all, absolutely not. 'Pantoute' is a strong, familiar negation.
You. 'Toé' is the familiar pronunciation of 'toi'.
Me. 'Moé' is the familiar pronunciation of 'moi'.

words.example_en: What do you want to drink?
words.meaning_en: A drink, a beverage. 'Breuvage' is standard in Quebec, old-fashioned in France.

words.example_en: Hand me that thing over there.
words.meaning_en: A thingamajig, a gadget, a thing whose name you forgot. Extremely useful word.

words.example_en: That movie was awesome! / That movie was disgusting!
words.meaning_en: Tricky: 'écoeurant' can mean disgusting OR amazing, depending on tone and context. Listen for the tone before you react.
Boring, flat, dull. 'Plate' is the Quebec word for boring — don't confuse it with a plate.
To fool around, waste time, or tease someone. Context decides which.
Fed up, tired of something. 'Tanné' is very Quebecois and very relatable in February.
Stupid, an idiot (as a noun for a person). Familiar insult — don't use it at work.

words.example_qc: Va tout drette, puis à gauche.
words.meaning_en: Straight ahead. 'Tout drette' is the familiar Quebec way to say 'tout droit'.
So far, up to now. 'À date' is a Quebec calque from English 'to date'.

words.example_en: Check if the bus is coming.
words.meaning_en: To check. 'Checker' is an anglicism verb, conjugated like a French verb, and totally normal here.
